mainTopic: Saying קריאת שמע and holy words near filth, bad smells, and urine: distances, doubts, and how dry is dry enough
overview: The amud opens by finishing a rule: for תפלה a person must cover his heart. רב הונא then rules that someone who walked into a בית הכסא wearing תפילין covers them with his hand until the first mass is out, since holding back is dangerous. Next, רב הונא and רב חסדא argue about saying קריאת שמע when part of the body is not clean, and then about how far to move from a bad smell. A ברייתא supports רב חסדא, but רבא rules like a different, shorter list of forbidden filth. רב ששת teaches that a smell with no visible source does not stop תורה learning, but it does stop קריאת שמע. אביי and רבא argue about filth that is passing by, and רב פפא says a pig's mouth counts as passing filth. רב יהודה rules on cases of doubt: a doubt about feces is strict, while a doubt about urine is lenient, because urine on the ground is only forbidden by the רבנן. The גמרא then asks how dry feces and urine must be before they stop forbidding holy words. רבא rules that feces as dry as earthenware is still forbidden, and urine forbids only while it is wet. The amud ends by testing that ruling against two ברייתות.

steps.title: For prayer, the heart must be covered
steps.stepSummary: The end of an earlier rule: for קריאת שמע less is needed, but for תפלה a person must cover his heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for prayer, he may not pray until he covers his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a rule that started earlier: for תפלה, a person must have his heart covered before he prays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the rule allowed saying קריאת שמע with a smaller covering. Here the גמרא adds that תפלה is stricter, because in תפלה a person stands and speaks directly to ה׳, so he must be properly covered.

phrases.english: But for prayer
[he may not pray] until he covers his heart.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל לִתְפִלָּה עַד שֶׁיְּכַסֶּה אֶת לִבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a rule that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For תפלה, one must cover his heart; קריאת שמע is more lenient.

steps.title: Entering a bathroom while wearing תפילין by mistake
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that someone who forgot and went into a בית הכסא wearing תפילין covers them with his hand until he finishes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: If someone forgot and went into the bathroom wearing תפילין, he puts his hand over them until he finishes.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives a new rule: if a person forgot and walked into a בית הכסא wearing תפילין, he covers them with his hand until he is finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, תפילין may not be brought into a בית הכסא. רב הונא gives a practical solution for someone already inside: covering the תפילין with his hand shows respect for them while he is stuck there.

keyTerms.meaning: תפילין, the boxes with פסוקים worn on the head and arm

phrases.english: And Rav Huna said:
If one forgot and entered the bathroom wearing tefillin —
he places his hand on them until he finishes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about תפילין in a בית הכסא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who entered a בית הכסא wearing תפילין by mistake covers them with his hand until he finishes.

steps.title: Can he really stay until he is completely done?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised: can it be that he stays inside with תפילין until he is totally finished?
steps.simpleTranslation: Until he finishes — can you really think that?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב הונא's words 'until he finishes.' It is hard to believe he may stay there wearing תפילין that long.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'until he finishes' sound like he may stay for the whole visit. That seems too lenient, since being in a בית הכסא with תפילין is not respectful. So the גמרא says this can't be what רב הונא meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Can it enter your mind? (would you really think so?)

phrases.english: Until he finishes — can that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of רב הונא's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words 'עַד שֶׁיִּגְמוֹר' in רב הונא's rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Staying the whole time in a בית הכסא with תפילין is too disrespectful to be allowed.

steps.title: Only until the first mass
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains 'until he finishes' with רב נחמן בר יצחק: only until the first mass of stool comes out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, as רב נחמן בר יצחק said: until he finishes the first mass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing רב הונא's words: he waits only until the first mass of stool is out, and then he leaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Until he finishes' does not mean the whole visit. It means only the first part, after which he can step out and take off the תפילין. This keeps the time with תפילין in the בית הכסא as short as possible.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'pillar'; here a mass of stool

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כִּדְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rather, as Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Until he finishes the first mass.
phrases.notes: Literally 'the first pillar'; it means the first mass of stool.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּדְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the meaning of the words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Until he finishes' meant staying the whole visit.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means only until the first mass of stool, and then he leaves.

steps.title: Why not stop right away?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: why wait at all? Let him stop right away and get up.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him stop immediately and get up!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again: once he remembers he is wearing תפילין, why not stop right away and walk out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even waiting for the first mass is still time spent with תפילין in a בית הכסא. The best way to respect the תפילין would seem to be stopping at once. So the גמרא asks why any waiting is allowed.

phrases.english: But let him stop immediately and get up!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: Allowing him to wait until the first mass.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Respect for the תפילין would require him to stop and leave right away.

steps.title: Holding it in is dangerous
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: holding back stool or urine causes serious illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, as it was taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says, a mass of stool held back brings a person to dropsy, and a stream of urine held back brings a person to jaundice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why he may not just stop: a ברייתא says that holding back stool or urine makes a person sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stopping in the middle can harm a person's health. Because of this danger, חז"ל did not require him to stop at once; he finishes the first mass and then leaves. This explains why רב הונא's rule allows a short wait.
steps.whatToRemember: A person who entered a בית הכסא with תפילין covers them with his hand, waits only until the first mass, and then leaves. He does not stop right away, because holding back is dangerous.

phrases.english: Because of [the teaching] of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר,
phrases.english: as it was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says,
a mass [of stool] that is held back —
brings a person to dropsy,
phrases.notes: Dropsy is an illness where the body swells up with fluid.

phrases.english: a stream [of urine] that is held back —
brings a person to jaundice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a health reason from a ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He should stop immediately out of respect for the תפילין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Stopping is dangerous to health, so he may finish the first mass first.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that חז"ל took a person's health into account even when dealing with respect for holy objects.

steps.title: A dispute: saying שמע when part of the body is not clean
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא and רב חסדא argue about someone with צואה on his skin, or whose hand is inside a בית הכסא: may he say קריאת שמע?
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: If there is feces on his skin, or his hand is placed inside the bathroom, רב הונא said: it is permitted to recite שמע. רב חסדא said: it is forbidden to recite שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new מחלוקת: if only part of a person's body is in an unclean state, רב הונא allows קריאת שמע and רב חסדא forbids it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the person's mouth and most of his body are fine; only one part of the body is involved with something unclean. The question is whether that one part matters. רב הונא says it does not, and רב חסדא says it does.

phrases.english: It was stated: [If there is] feces on his skin,
or his hand is placed in the bathroom,

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא אָמַר: מוּתָּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Rav Huna said: It is permitted to recite Shema.

phrases.aramaic: רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: אָסוּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: It is forbidden to recite Shema.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, a מחלוקת between רב הונא and רב חסדא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא: one may say קריאת שמע; רב חסדא: one may not.

steps.title: רב הונא's source: every soul praises
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains רב הונא's reason from the פסוק 'כל הנשמה תהלל יה': what matters is the breath, the mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What is רב הונא's reason? Because it is written: 'Let every soul praise the Lord, Halleluyah.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the source for רב הונא's lenient view: a פסוק that ties praise of ה׳ to the נשמה, the breath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא reads נשמה as connected to breathing. Praise comes from the breath and the mouth, so as long as the mouth is in a clean place, the rest of the body does not stop him from saying קריאת שמע.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַב הוּנָא —
phrases.english: Rava said: What is the reason of Rav Huna?
As it is written: "Let every soul praise the Lord, Halleluyah."
phrases.notes: תהלים 150:6. He reads נשמה like breath, so praise depends on the mouth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רב הונא's view in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's ruling that one may say קריאת שמע.

steps.title: רב חסדא's source: all my bones praise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats רב חסדא's view and brings his source: 'כל עצמותי תאמרנה', praise comes from the whole body.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: It is forbidden to recite שמע. What is רב חסדא's reason? Because it is written: 'All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like You.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source for רב חסדא's strict view: a פסוק that says all of a person's bones praise ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If praise comes from the entire body, then every part of the body must be in a clean state. So even one hand in a בית הכסא, or צואה on the skin, stops a person from saying קריאת שמע.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא: praise depends on the mouth (כל הנשמה), so he may say שמע. רב חסדא: praise comes from the whole body (כל עצמותי), so he may not.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: אָסוּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said: It is forbidden to recite Shema.
What is the reason of Rav Chisda?

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״כׇּל עַצְמוֹתַי תֹּאמַרְנָה ה׳ מִי כָמוֹךָ״.
phrases.english: As it is written: "All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like You."
phrases.notes: תהלים 35:10.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the other side of the מחלוקת, matching step 8.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's ruling that one may not say קריאת שמע.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two פסוקים show the real root of the argument: does praising ה׳ depend only on the mouth, or on the whole body?

steps.title: How far to move from a bad smell that has a source
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says to move four אמות from the source of the smell. רב חסדא says to move four אמות from the place where the smell stops.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: if there is a bad smell coming from something you can see, רב הונא says a person moves four אמות away and then says קריאת שמע. רב חסדא says he moves four אמות past the point where the smell ends, and then says קריאת שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new argument between רב הונא and רב חסדא about saying קריאת שמע near a bad smell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree that one must move away from a smell that has a visible source. They argue about where to start counting. For רב הונא you count from the thing itself. For רב חסדא you count from where the smell runs out, which can mean moving much farther.

keyTerms.meaning: A source, the actual thing you can see that gives off the smell
Four אמות, roughly six to eight feet

phrases.aramaic: אִתְּמַר: רֵיחַ רַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עִיקָּר —
phrases.english: It was said: a bad smell that has a source —

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא אָמַר: מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת,
phrases.english: Rav Huna said: he moves four amos away,
phrases.notes: For רב הונא, you count the four אמות from the source itself.

phrases.english: and recites Shema.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת
phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said: he moves four amos away
from the place where the smell stopped,
and recites Shema.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: רֵיחַ רַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עִיקָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the argument about filth on the body or a hand inside a בית הכסא, the גמרא brings a second argument between the same two אמוראים, this time about a bad smell.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא: move four אמות from the source of the smell. רב חסדא: move four אמות from where the smell ends.

steps.title: A ברייתא that supports רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists kinds of filth that one may not say קריאת שמע near, gives rules about height and distance, and ends by saying to move four אמות from the place of the smell, just like רב חסדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that matches רב חסדא: A person may not say קריאת שמע facing human waste, dog waste, pig waste, chicken waste, or a garbage heap that smells bad. If the waste is in a spot ten טפחים higher or ten טפחים lower than him, he may sit next to it and say קריאת שמע. If not, he must move away until he can no longer see it. The same is true for תפילה. For a bad smell that has a source, he moves four אמות from the place of the smell and says קריאת שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רב חסדא. The last line of the ברייתא is the part that matches him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says to move four אמות 'from the place of the smell.' That means counting from where the smell is felt, not from the filth itself, which is רב חסדא's view. Along the way, the ברייתא also teaches that a ten-טפחים height difference separates a person from the filth, and that otherwise he must move until it is out of sight.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with him
As far as his eyes can see, meaning until it is out of sight

steps.confusionAlert: Two different distances appear here. For filth you can see, you move until it is out of sight. For a bad smell, you move four אמות from where the smell is. Don't mix them up.

phrases.english: It was taught in accordance with Rav Chisda:
A person may not recite Shema,
not facing human excrement,
and not facing dog excrement,
and not facing pig excrement,
and not facing chicken excrement,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא כְּנֶגֶד צוֹאַת אַשְׁפָּה שֶׁרֵיחָהּ רָע.
phrases.english: and not facing the filth of a dung heap that smells bad.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם הָיָה מָקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים
phrases.english: And if it was in a place ten handbreadths higher
or ten handbreadths lower —
he may sit beside it and recite Shema.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו — מַרְחִיק מִמֶּנּוּ מְלוֹא עֵינָיו.
phrases.english: And if not, he moves away from it until it is beyond his sight.
And the same applies to prayer.
A bad smell that has a source —
he moves four amos away from the place of the smell,
and recites Shema.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support from a ברייתא for רב חסדא's side of the argument in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's view that one counts four אמות from where the smell ends
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא whose last line says to move four אמות 'from the place of the smell'

steps.title: רבא rules like a different, more lenient ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the הלכה does not follow the ברייתא just quoted in all its rulings. It follows another ברייתא that forbids only human waste, and pig or dog waste that hides were put into.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה is not like this ברייתא in all of these rulings. Rather, it is like this other ברייתא: A person may not say קריאת שמע facing human waste, or pig waste or dog waste when hides were placed in them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the final הלכה and picks a different ברייתא with a shorter list of forbidden filth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא forbade all dog and pig waste, chicken waste, and a smelly garbage heap. The second ברייתא forbids only human waste, and pig or dog waste used for tanning hides. So the הלכה is more lenient than the first ברייתא's list.

keyTerms.meaning: The הלכה is not like this
A taught source, here meaning the ברייתא just quoted

steps.whyThisMatters: This step tells us the practical הלכה about which kinds of filth stop a person from saying קריאת שמע.

phrases.english: Rava said: The halacha is not

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא מַתְנִיתָא בְּכָל הָנֵי שְׁמַעְתָּתָא,
phrases.english: like this baraita in all of these rulings,
but rather like that which was taught:
A person may not recite Shema
not facing human excrement,
and not facing pig excrement,
and not facing dog excrement
when he placed hides into them.
phrases.notes: Hides were soaked in this kind of waste as part of tanning them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לֵית הִלְכְתָא כִּי הָא מַתְנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets aside the list in the ברייתא from step 11 for practical הלכה and replaces it with another ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows the second ברייתא: one may not say קריאת שמע facing human waste, or pig or dog waste that hides were placed in.

steps.title: What about a bad smell with no source
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת is asked what the law is for a bad smell that has no visible source.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב ששת: What is the law for a bad smell that has no source?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a new question: until now we dealt with a smell that has a visible source, and now they ask about one that doesn't.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a visible source, everyone agreed one must move away. A smell with no source you can see may be treated more leniently, so they ask רב ששת. His answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: That has no source you can see

phrases.english: They asked Rav Sheshet:

phrases.aramaic: רֵיחַ רַע שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עִיקָּר, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: A bad smell that has no source, what is the law?
phrases.notes: Think of passed gas: there's a smell, but nothing you can see.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a smell with a source (steps 10-11) to a smell without one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a bad smell with no visible source stops a person from learning or saying קריאת שמע

steps.title: רב ששת points to the mats in the בית מדרש
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers from what people actually do: in the בית מדרש some sleep on the mats while others keep learning.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Come and see these mats in the בית מדרש, where some people sleep and some people learn.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the question by pointing to what really happens in the בית מדרש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sleepers sometimes give off smells that have no source, yet the people next to them keep learning and no one stops them. This shows that a smell with no source does not stop תורה learning.

phrases.english: He said to them: Come and see
these mats of the study hall,
where these sleep and these study.
phrases.notes: The ones sleeping may give off smells, yet the ones learning beside them keep going.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְהוּ: אֲתוֹ חֲזוֹ הָנֵי צִיפֵּי דְבֵי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A smell with no source does not stop learning, as we see from the בית מדרש where people learn beside those sleeping.

steps.title: The answer only covers תורה learning and someone else's smell
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רב ששת's answer: it applies to דברי תורה, not קריאת שמע. Even for דברי תורה, it applies only when the smell came from someone else, not from the person himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to תורה learning, but not to קריאת שמע. And even for תורה learning we only said this when the smell comes from his friend, but not when it comes from himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes by narrowing רב ששת's answer in two ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, the leniency is only for learning, not for קריאת שמע. Second, even for learning, it only applies when the smell came from someone else. If the person himself made the smell, he may not learn.

keyTerms.meaning: And these words apply only to...
Of his friend, coming from another person

steps.whatToRemember: A smell with no visible source does not stop someone from learning תורה if it came from another person. But it does stop קריאת שמע, and it stops learning if it came from the person himself.

phrases.english: And this applies only to Torah study,
but for the recitation of Shema, no.
And even regarding Torah study we only said this
when it is from his friend,
but from himself, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the leniency that came out of רב ששת's answer in step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A smell with no source is permitted only for תורה learning, and only when it came from someone else. It is not permitted for קריאת שמע, and not for learning when the smell came from oneself.

steps.title: אביי and רבא argue about filth that is passing by
steps.stepSummary: A מחלוקת is stated: for צואה עוברת (filth that is moving past), אביי permits saying קריאת שמע and רבא forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: about filth that is passing by, אביי says it is allowed to say קריאת שמע, and רבא says it is forbidden to say קריאת שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new מחלוקת. אביי and רבא argue about saying קריאת שמע near filth that is moving and not sitting in one place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the סוגיא spoke about filth or a smell that stays in one spot. Here the new question is whether filth that is only moving past also forbids קריאת שמע. אביי says no and רבא says yes.

keyTerms.meaning: Filth that is passing by and not resting in one place

phrases.english: It was stated: filth that is passing by —

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי אָמַר: מוּתָּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Abaye said: It is permitted to recite Shema.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא אָמַר: אָסוּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Rava said: It is forbidden to recite Shema.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question after the discussion of a smell with no visible source
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: one may say קריאת שמע near passing filth. רבא: one may not.

steps.title: אביי brings a proof from a מצורע under a tree
steps.stepSummary: אביי proves his view from a משנה: a מצורע makes a person under a tree טמא only when the מצורע is standing there, not when he is just passing. The same is true of a stone with צרעת.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: How do I know this? Because the משנה teaches: if a טמא person is standing under a tree and a טהור person passes under it, the טהור one becomes טמא. If a טהור person is standing under the tree and a טמא person passes under it, the טהור one stays טהור. But if the טמא one stops there, the טהור one becomes טמא. The same is true for a stone with צרעת.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a משנה to support his view that something only passing by does not have the full effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a מצורע, the טומאה spreads under the tree only when the מצורע is standing still. When he just passes, it does not spread. אביי says filth works the same way: if it only passes, it does not forbid קריאת שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do I say this? (an אמורא brings a source for his own view)
A stone with צרעת, from a house that has צרעת

phrases.english: Abaye said: From where do I say this?
As we learned: If the impure one is standing under the tree
phrases.notes: The impure one here is a מצורע, someone with צרעת.

phrases.english: and the pure one passes by, he is impure.
If the pure one is standing under the tree
and the impure one passes by, he stays pure.
And if the impure one stopped there, the pure one is impure.
And the same is true for a stone with tzara'at.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source for אביי's side of the מחלוקת
steps.raayaObject: אביי's ruling that passing filth does not forbid קריאת שמע
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about a מצורע and a stone with צרעת: they spread טומאה only when standing still, not when passing

steps.title: רבא explains why the מצורע case is different
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that for a מצורע the law depends on a fixed place, as the פסוק speaks of his 'dwelling'. For קריאת שמע the Torah requires that 'your camp shall be holy', and when filth passes by, the camp is not holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא would tell you: There, the matter depends on staying in a fixed place, as it is written: 'He shall dwell alone, outside the camp shall his dwelling be.' Here, the Torah said: 'Your camp shall be holy', and that is missing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes away אביי's proof by showing that the two cases depend on different things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about a מצורע talks about where he 'dwells', so his טומאה is tied to a place where he stays. The rule for קריאת שמע comes from 'your camp shall be holy', and passing filth still makes the camp not holy. So the משנה about a מצורע proves nothing about filth.

keyTerms.meaning: And רבא would say to you: his answer to the other side's proof
'Your camp shall be holy': the source for keeping filth away during holy words
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: And Rava would say to you:
There, the matter depends on being in a fixed place,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the case of the מצורע under the tree.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'He shall dwell alone,
outside the camp shall his dwelling be.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 13:46

phrases.english: Here, the Torah said: 'Your camp shall be holy,'
phrases.notes: דברים 23:15

phrases.english: and that is not the case here.
phrases.notes: He means that while filth is passing by, the camp is not holy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's proof from the מצורע
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not deny that a passing מצורע does not make others טמא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The laws of a מצורע depend on a fixed dwelling place. The laws of קריאת שמע depend on the camp being holy, and moving filth still spoils that.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי compares passing filth to a passing מצורע, which has no effect. רבא says the two are different: a מצורע's law depends on a fixed place, but 'your camp shall be holy' is broken even by filth that is only passing by.

steps.title: רב פפא: a pig's mouth is like passing filth
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that a pig's mouth is treated like צואה עוברת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: A pig's mouth is like filth that is passing by.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds a new ruling connected to the topic of passing filth: a pig's mouth counts as moving filth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pig's mouth is always dirty, and the pig keeps moving around. So רב פפא puts it in the same group as צואה עוברת. The law for it would then follow the מחלוקת of אביי and רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Is like, is considered the same as

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
A pig's mouth is like filth that is passing by.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: פִּי חֲזִיר כְּצוֹאָה עוֹבֶרֶת דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the category of צואה עוברת from the מחלוקת to define a new case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pig's mouth counts as צואה עוברת.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב פפא needs to say this, since it seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: everyone knows a pig's mouth is dirty, so why did he need to teach it? This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אמורא does not usually teach something everyone already knows. So the גמרא asks what new thing רב פפא is teaching us.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! (the גמרא asks why a ruling needs to be said)

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רב פפא's ruling teaches anything new
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that a pig's mouth is like passing filth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A pig's mouth is plainly dirty, so the ruling seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Even right after the pig comes out of the river
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב פפא teaches that a pig's mouth counts as filth even after the pig has come up from the river.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for when the pig has just come up from the river.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing the new point in רב פפא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think that after the pig comes up from the river, its mouth has been washed clean. רב פפא teaches that it still counts as passing filth. That is the new point.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case: shows the new point of a ruling

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for when the pig has come up from the river.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא אַף עַל גַּב דְּסָלֵיק מִנַּהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' question
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a case where the ruling is not obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: After the pig comes up from the river, its mouth might be clean.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even then, a pig's mouth counts as passing filth.
steps.whatToRemember: A pig's mouth always counts as צואה עוברת, even right after the pig comes out of the river.

steps.title: Doubtful feces is forbidden, doubtful urine is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that if we are unsure whether there is צואה, it is forbidden to say holy words. If we are unsure whether there is מי רגלים, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: If you are not sure whether there is feces nearby, it is forbidden to say holy words there. If you are not sure whether there is urine nearby, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רב יהודה about cases of doubt: we do not know whether filth is present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the סוגיא dealt with filth that was really there, either still or passing by. Now רב יהודה adds the case of doubt, and he treats the two kinds of filth differently. A doubt about feces makes us strict, but a doubt about urine lets us be lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: A doubt; a case where we are not sure

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
A doubt about feces: it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: He means it is forbidden to say קריאת שמע or other holy words near it.

phrases.english: A doubt about urine: it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: סְפֵק צוֹאָה — אֲסוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, cases of doubt, after the discussion of passing filth and a pig's mouth.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A doubt about feces is forbidden. A doubt about urine is permitted.

steps.title: Second version of רב יהודה's ruling: house versus garbage heap
steps.stepSummary: Another version of רב יהודה's ruling. A doubt about feces is permitted in a house but forbidden in a garbage heap. A doubt about urine is permitted even in a garbage heap.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב יהודה said it differently. If you are not sure about feces: in a house it is permitted, but in a garbage heap it is forbidden. If you are not sure about urine: it is permitted even in a garbage heap.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same ruling from רב יהודה, and this version is more lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, a doubt about feces depends on the place. A house is usually clean, so we may assume nothing is there. A garbage heap usually has filth, so we are strict. A doubt about urine is permitted everywhere, so in both versions urine is the more lenient case.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion that argues with רב יהודה. It is another report of what רב יהודה himself said.

phrases.english: Some say:
Rav Yehuda said:
A doubt about feces: in a house, it is permitted,
in a garbage heap, it is forbidden.
A doubt about urine:
even in a garbage heap, it is also permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, more lenient version of the ruling in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A doubt about feces is permitted in a house and forbidden in a garbage heap. A doubt about urine is permitted even in a garbage heap.

steps.title: Source for the urine leniency: רב המנונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב יהודה follows רב המנונא, who said the Torah only forbade holy words facing the stream of urine.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה holds like רב המנונא, who said: the Torah only forbade it facing the stream of urine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts explaining why רב יהודה is lenient about a doubt with urine. The first reason is רב המנונא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב המנונא says that the Torah's prohibition on urine applies only while the stream is flowing. Urine that is already on the ground is not forbidden by the Torah. That is why a doubt about it can be treated lightly.

phrases.aramaic: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא,
phrases.english: He holds like this teaching of Rav Hamnuna,
phrases.notes: 'He' is רב יהודה. The גמרא is explaining his leniency about urine.

phrases.english: for Rav Hamnuna said:
The Torah did not forbid it
except facing the stream alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind the urine leniency in both versions of רב יהודה.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's leniency about a doubt with urine
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב המנונא: the Torah only forbade facing the stream of urine

steps.title: רבי יונתן points out two פסוקים that seem to contradict
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה also follows רבי יונתן. רבי יונתן noted that one פסוק only says to go outside the camp, while another פסוק says you must also cover your waste.
steps.simpleTranslation: He also holds like רבי יונתן. רבי יונתן pointed out a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there.' Another פסוק says: 'You shall have a spade... and you shall cover your waste.'
steps.whatsHappening: This step sets up a contradiction between two פסוקים. The answer comes in the next step, and it will show the Torah source for being lenient with urine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק only requires going outside the camp and says nothing about covering. The second פסוק requires covering with a spade. Both speak about relieving oneself, so the question is which rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: He pointed out a contradiction (between two sources)
A spade or peg for digging

phrases.english: And he holds like Rabbi Yonatan.
For Rabbi Yonatan pointed out a contradiction:
It is written: 'You shall have a place outside the camp
phrases.notes: דברים 23:13. Here 'יד' means a place.

phrases.english: and you shall go out there, outside,'
and it is written: 'And you shall have a spade, etc.
phrases.notes: דברים 23:14. 'וגו׳' means the פסוק goes on, and only its key ending is quoted.

phrases.english: and you shall cover your waste.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second source for רב יהודה's view, starting with a contradiction between פסוקים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק requires only going outside the camp, without covering. The other requires covering. They seem to clash.

steps.title: One פסוק is about feces, the other about urine
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן resolves it: the פסוק that requires covering is about צואה, and the פסוק that does not is about מי רגלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does this fit? Here it is speaking about feces, and there it is speaking about urine.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן answers the contradiction from the previous step by assigning each פסוק to a different kind of waste.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feces must be covered, so the 'cover your waste' פסוק is about feces. Urine does not need covering, so the 'just go outside' פסוק is about urine. Once we see that the Torah does not require covering urine, the Torah's concern with it must be limited.

keyTerms.meaning: How can this be? A formula that opens a resolution

phrases.english: How can this be?
Here it is about the 'big' needs, here about the 'small' needs.
phrases.notes: The covering פסוק is about feces. The 'just go outside' פסוק is about urine.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד? כָּאן בִּגְדוֹלִים, כָּאן בִּקְטַנִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each פסוק refers to a different kind of waste
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both פסוקים seemed to speak about the same waste, so they seemed to clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: The covering פסוק is about feces. The פסוק without covering is about urine.

steps.title: Urine on the ground is only rabbinic, so a doubt is permitted
steps.stepSummary: The conclusion: by Torah law urine is only forbidden facing the stream. Once it is on the ground, only the רבנן forbade it, and they did not make that גזירה in a case of doubt.
steps.simpleTranslation: So with urine, the Torah only forbade it facing the stream. Once it has fallen to the ground, it is permitted by Torah law. The רבנן made a decree about it, but they only did so when the urine is certainly there. When it is only a doubt, they did not make a decree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pulls everything together. It explains why רב יהודה permits a doubt about urine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the Torah does not require covering urine, its prohibition is only on the flowing stream, just as רב המנונא said. Urine on the ground is forbidden only by the רבנן. They limited their own גזירה to cases where the urine is certainly there, so a doubt stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: So we see; this shows that
They decreed; made a rabbinic גזירה
When they are certainly there / when there is only a doubt

steps.whatToRemember: Feces: Torah-level, so even a doubt is strict, at least in a garbage heap. Urine: the Torah only forbade facing the flowing stream. Once it is on the ground, it is a rabbinic גזירה, and the רבנן did not apply it to a doubt.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in הלכה: when a prohibition is only rabbinic, the רבנן often did not extend it to cases of doubt.

phrases.english: So we see that with urine,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אָסְרָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא כְּנֶגֶד עַמּוּד בִּלְבַד.
phrases.english: the Torah forbade it only facing the stream alone.
But once it has fallen to the ground, it is permitted,
and it is the Rabbis who made a decree about it,
and when the Rabbis made the decree, it was only where it is certain,
but where it is a doubt, they did not decree.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא קְטַנִּים לֹא אָסְרָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא כְּנֶגֶד עַמּוּד בִּלְבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from רבי יונתן's resolution and ties it back to רב המנונא and רב יהודה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Urine on the ground is forbidden only by the רבנן, and only when it is certainly there. So a doubt about urine is permitted, which explains רב יהודה's ruling.

steps.title: How long does certain urine stay forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long urine that is definitely present still forbids saying holy words.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when the urine is definitely there, until when is it forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new question. We know a doubt about urine is permitted, so now it asks about urine we know is there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 explained that once urine is on the ground, only the רבנן forbade it, and not in a case of doubt. That leaves an open question: when the urine is certainly there, at what point does that rabbinic ban end?

keyTerms.meaning: Certain, definite (the opposite of a doubt)

phrases.english: And with their certain cases, until when?
phrases.notes: He means urine we know is there, as opposed to the doubt case from step 23.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from doubtful urine, which is permitted, to certain urine, and asks how long its ban lasts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The time or state at which certain urine on the ground no longer forbids saying holy words.

steps.title: Three אמוראים: as long as it is still wet
steps.stepSummary: שמואל, רבי יוחנן, and עולא all say urine forbids holy words as long as it is wet enough to wet your hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: as long as it moistens. So too רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: as long as it moistens. So too עולא said: as long as it moistens.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with one rule, said by three different אמוראים: the urine is forbidden only while it is still wet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether touching the spot would make your hand wet. Once it has dried that much, even if a stain is left, these אמוראים allow saying holy words there. Bringing three sources shows how widely this view was held.

keyTerms.meaning: It moistens, wet enough to wet the hand that touches it
And so too said (another sage agrees)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
As long as it moistens.
phrases.notes: He means it is still wet enough that your hand would get wet if you touched it.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And so too Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
As long as it moistens.
And so too Ulla said:
As long as it moistens.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Certain urine forbids holy words only while it is still wet enough to wet the hand.

steps.title: גניבא quotes רב: as long as its mark can be seen
steps.stepSummary: גניבא says in the name of רב that urine forbids holy words as long as its mark on the ground can still be seen.
steps.simpleTranslation: גניבא said in the name of רב: as long as its mark is visible.
steps.whatsHappening: A different, stricter opinion is brought. According to גניבא, רב held that even dry urine is forbidden while its stain is still visible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is stricter than the three אמוראים in step 29. They stop the ban once the spot is dry; גניבא's version of רב keeps the ban as long as any visible stain remains.

phrases.english: Geniva said in the name of Rav:
As long as its mark is visible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a stricter answer to the same question, disagreeing with step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to גניבא's report of רב, urine forbids holy words as long as its mark on the ground can be seen.

steps.title: רב יוסף: רב could not have said this
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף argues that גניבא misquoted רב, since רב permits crusted feces, so dried urine should surely be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: May his Master forgive גניבא! After all, about feces, רב יהודה said in the name of רב that once its surface has formed a crust, it is permitted. Is there any question about urine?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges גניבא's quote. He uses a different statement of רב to show that רב was lenient, so he could not have been this strict about urine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feces is more serious than urine, since the תורה requires covering feces (step 26). If רב permits feces once it has a dry crust, then dried urine should be permitted all the more. So גניבא's strict quote must be wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: May his Master (God) forgive him, a strong way of saying he made a mistake
Now, if even (opens a 'how much more so' argument)
Is it even a question? (it is obvious)

steps.confusionAlert: It is the same רב יהודה both times, quoting two different teachers. Here he quotes רב about feces; in step 29 he quoted שמואל about urine.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
May his Master forgive Geniva,
phrases.notes: Literally 'his Master should let him off,' a polite but sharp way of saying גניבא got רב's words wrong.

phrases.english: Now, if regarding feces,
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said
once its surface has formed a crust, it is permitted,
is there any question about urine?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף שְׁרָא לֵיהּ מָרֵיהּ לִגְנִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the accuracy of גניבא's quote in step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: גניבא's report that רב forbids urine as long as its mark is visible.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from another statement of רב: if feces, which is more serious, is permitted once crusted, then dried urine must be permitted, so רב could not have said what גניבא reports.

steps.title: אביי: רב also has a strict statement about feces
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that רב has another statement forbidding even feces as dry as earthenware, so גניבא's strict version fits.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Why did you choose to rely on that statement? Rely on this one! For רבה בר רב הונא said in the name of רב: feces, even when it is like earthenware, is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back on רב יוסף's attack. He points to a different quote of רב that is strict about dry feces, which supports גניבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two reports of רב about dry feces: one lenient (crusted is permitted) and one strict (even like earthenware is forbidden). רב יוסף's proof only works with the lenient one. If we follow the strict one, it makes sense that רב would also forbid urine while its mark is visible, just as גניבא said.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? (why did you choose this over that?)
Like earthenware, dried hard like a piece of pottery

steps.whatToRemember: There are two traditions of רב about dry feces, one lenient and one strict. גניבא's strict view on urine matches the strict tradition, so רב יוסף's attack is not a must.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
What did you see that you relied on that one?
phrases.notes: 'That one' is רב's lenient statement about crusted feces from step 31.

phrases.english: Rely on this one,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: as Rabba bar Rav Huna said that Rav said:
Feces, even when it is like earthenware, is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי מַאי חָזֵית דְּסָמְכַתְּ אַהָא סְמוֹךְ אַהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's challenge by bringing a stricter tradition of רב.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב יוסף's proof that רב could not have said גניבא's ruling.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב יוסף chose only one of two reports of רב; the other report is strict about dry feces and supports גניבא.

steps.title: What counts as feces 'like earthenware'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how dry feces must be to count as 'like earthenware'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the case of feces like earthenware?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a definition. It wants to know exactly what 'like earthenware' in רב's statement means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב forbade feces 'even like earthenware,' but that phrase is not exact. The גמרא now asks for a clear test.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: And what is the case of feces like earthenware?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to define a term from רב's statement in step 32.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact physical state of feces called 'like earthenware'.

steps.title: The test: it does not crumble when thrown or rolled
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says it is 'like earthenware' as long as it does not crumble when thrown; others say, when rolled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: as long as one throws it and it does not crumble. And some say: as long as one rolls it and it does not crumble.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a physical test for 'like earthenware.' There are two versions: throwing it, or rolling it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As long as the feces holds together and does not fall apart, it counts as 'like earthenware' and is still forbidden. The two versions differ on the test: throwing is a harder test than rolling, so the versions differ on how strong it must be to still count.
steps.whatToRemember: Feces is 'like earthenware' and still forbidden as long as it holds together. One version tests by throwing it, another by rolling it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
As long as one throws it and it does not crumble.
And some say:
As long as one rolls it and it does not crumble.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁזּוֹרְקָה וְאֵינָהּ נִפְרֶכֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the definition question of step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Feces is 'like earthenware' as long as it does not crumble when thrown, or in the second version, when rolled.

steps.title: רבינא's story: checking whether feces had dried
steps.stepSummary: רבינא tells that רב יהודה מדיפתי saw feces and told him to check whether its surface had formed a crust. Another version says he told him to check whether it had cracked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: I was standing before רב יהודה מדיפתי when he saw feces. He told me: Check whether its surface has formed a crust or not. Some say he told him: Check whether it has cracked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real-life story showing how a rabbi checked whether feces was dry enough to stop forbidding holy words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story adds a practical test for dryness. In one version, a dry crust on the surface is enough. In the other version, the feces must actually be cracked, which is a stricter test.

phrases.english: Ravina said:

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה קָאֵימְנָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה מִדִּיפְתִּי
phrases.english: I was standing before Rav Yehuda of Difti
He saw feces, and he said to me:

phrases.aramaic: עַיֵּין אִי קָרְמוּ פָּנֶיהָ אִי לָא.
phrases.english: Check whether its surface has formed a crust or not.
Some say that this is what he said to him:
Check whether it has cracked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a practical test, from a real event, for how dry feces must be.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Feces is checked for dryness, either by seeing whether a crust has formed or, in another version, whether it has cracked.

steps.title: What is the final ruling?
steps.stepSummary: After all these opinions, the גמרא asks what the final ruling is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was concluded about this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask for the bottom line. This sets up the next move, where it brings a dispute and a final ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Several conflicting statements have come up about dried feces and urine. The גמרא now wants to know which view is the actual הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the conclusion about it?

phrases.english: What was concluded about this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a final ruling after the earlier mixed opinions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The final הלכה about feces as dry as earthenware, and about urine.

steps.title: Dispute about feces dry like earthenware
steps.stepSummary: אמימר says feces as dry as earthenware is forbidden, and מר זוטרא says it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: about feces as dry as earthenware, אמימר said it is forbidden, and מר זוטרא said it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: In answer, the גמרא brings a recorded argument between two אמוראים about very dry feces.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sides match the two versions of רב from earlier. אמימר is like the version where even earthenware-dry feces forbids, and מר זוטרא is like the version that permits dried feces.

keyTerms.meaning: Like earthenware, meaning hard and dry

phrases.english: It was stated: about feces that is like earthenware,
Ameimar said: It is forbidden,
and Mar Zutra said: It is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question by bringing a dispute.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is a dispute: אמימר forbids and מר זוטרא permits.

steps.title: רבא's ruling on dry feces and on urine
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that feces as dry as earthenware is forbidden, and urine forbids only as long as it is still wet.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה is that feces as dry as earthenware is forbidden, and urine forbids as long as it is still wet.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the final ruling: strict about dry feces, but more lenient about urine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For feces, רבא sides with אמימר. For urine, he does not follow the strict version of רב that forbids while the mark can be seen. Once the urine is no longer wet, it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Still wet, wet enough to make something else wet

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's הלכה: feces as dry as earthenware is still forbidden; urine forbids only while it is still wet.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rulings. רבא is strict about dry feces but more lenient about urine than גניבא's report from step 30.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical ruling, and the next steps test it against a ברייתא.

phrases.english: Rava said: The halakha is:
Feces like earthenware is forbidden,
and urine, as long as it is still wet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute and adds a ruling about urine.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Feces as dry as earthenware forbids; urine forbids only while it is wet.

steps.title: A ברייתא suggests a visible urine mark still forbids
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says urine that soaked in or dried up is permitted. The גמרא reads 'soaked in' as being like 'dried up,' where no mark is left. That would mean urine with a visible mark is forbidden even when it is no longer wet, against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: Urine, as long as it is wet, is forbidden. If it soaked in or dried up, it is permitted. Isn't 'soaked in' like 'dried up'? Just as dried-up urine leaves no visible mark, so too soaked-in urine means no visible mark is left. So if its mark can be seen, it is forbidden, even though it is no longer wet!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's lenient ruling on urine by drawing an inference from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא puts 'soaked in' next to 'dried up.' If both mean the mark is gone, then the only permitted case is when no mark remains. That supports the strict view that a visible mark forbids, and goes against רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to, in the same way as
Its mark can still be seen

phrases.aramaic: מֵיתִיבִי: מֵי רַגְלַיִם כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין — אֲסוּרִין,
phrases.english: They challenged: Urine, as long as it is wet, is forbidden;
if it soaked in or dried up, it is permitted.
Isn't 'soaked in' similar to 'dried up'?
Just as when it dried up, its mark cannot be seen,
so too 'soaked in' means its mark cannot be seen.
So if its mark can be seen, it is forbidden,
even though it is no longer wet!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: מֵי רַגְלַיִם כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's ruling that urine forbids only while wet.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that urine stops forbidding once it is no longer wet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By comparing 'soaked in' to 'dried up,' the ברייתא permits only when no mark is left. So a visible mark should forbid even without wetness.

steps.title: The opening clause of the ברייתא points the other way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the first clause of the ברייתא suggests the opposite: only wet urine is forbidden, so urine with a visible mark is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And by your reasoning, read the first clause: 'As long as it is wet' it is forbidden. That means if only its mark can be seen, it is permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back by drawing an opposite inference from the beginning of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause makes wetness the only thing that forbids, which implies a dry visible mark is permitted. That clashes with the inference from the last clause. So the challenge's inference is not stronger than the opposite one.

phrases.english: And by your reasoning, read the first clause:
Only 'as long as it is wet' is it forbidden,
which means if only its mark can be seen, it is permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by showing the ברייתא's first clause implies the opposite.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the ברייתא's last clause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The inference from the last clause is contradicted by an equally strong inference from the first clause.

steps.title: No proof can be drawn from this ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: Since the two clauses point in opposite directions, the גמרא concludes that nothing can be learned from this ברייתא about a visible mark.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, nothing can be learned from this ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the challenge: the ברייתא cannot decide the question, so רבא's ruling stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each clause leads to a different inference about urine that is dry but still leaves a mark. Because they cancel each other out, the ברייתא proves nothing either way. The challenge to רבא falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Nothing can be learned from it

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא cannot prove whether a visible urine mark forbids, because its two clauses point opposite ways. רבא's ruling (forbidden only while wet) is not disproved.

phrases.english: Rather, nothing can be learned from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the result of the opposite inferences: the ברייתא proves nothing.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא gives no proof about a visible urine mark, so רבא's ruling stands.

steps.title: Suggesting the question is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that the question of a visible urine mark is an old dispute, and quotes a ברייתא where the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי disagree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is a dispute between תנאים. It is forbidden to say קריאת שמע opposite a vessel that urine was poured out of. Urine itself that was poured out: if it soaked in, it is permitted; if it did not soak in, it is forbidden. רבי יוסי says: it is forbidden as long as it is still wet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new idea: maybe the question of a visible mark was already argued about by תנאים. It quotes a ברייתא to look at closely in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has two opinions about poured-out urine. The תנא קמא uses the words 'soaked in / did not soak in,' and רבי יוסי uses 'as long as it is wet.' The גמרא will now try to figure out if these two wordings really mean different things.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say this is like a dispute between תנאים
Soaked in (were absorbed into the ground)
Still wet enough to make something else wet
The first, unnamed opinion in a ברייתא or משנה

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of the Tannaim:
A vessel from which urine was poured out,
it is forbidden to read Shema opposite it.
And the urine itself that was poured out,
if it soaked in, it is permitted;
if it did not soak in, it is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: it is forbidden as long as it is still wet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 41 found no answer in the earlier ברייתא, the גמרא tries a different ברייתא where the question may be a dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ברייתא: the תנא קמא forbids poured urine that did not soak in; רבי יוסי forbids it as long as it is wet.

steps.title: What do 'soaked in' and 'did not soak in' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the תנא קמא means by 'soaked in' and 'did not soak in.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What does the תנא קמא mean by 'soaked in' and 'did not soak in'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the words of the תנא קמא. This sets up the next two steps, which try out two possible meanings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי disagree depends on what 'soaked in' means. If it means 'no longer wet,' they say the same thing. If it means 'no mark left,' they disagree about a visible mark.

keyTerms.meaning: What is / what does it mean

phrases.english: What is "soaked in" and what is "did not soak in"
that the first Tanna says?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״נִבְלְעוּ״ וּמַאי ״לֹא נִבְלְעוּ״ דְּקָאָמַר תַּנָּא קַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the key words in the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact meaning of נבלעו and לא נבלעו in the words of the תנא קמא.

steps.title: If 'soaked in' means 'no longer wet,' there is no dispute
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries reading 'soaked in' as 'no longer wet,' but rejects it because then רבי יוסי would be saying the same thing as the תנא קמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say 'soaked in' means it is no longer wet, and 'did not soak in' means it is still wet, and רבי יוסי comes to say that only while it is wet is it forbidden, but if only a mark is visible it is permitted, then רבי יוסי is the same as the תנא קמא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first possible meaning and throws it out. Under this reading the two opinions would say exactly the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'did not soak in' means 'still wet,' then both the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי forbid only wet urine. But רבי יוסי is quoted as arguing, so his words must add something new. This reading cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a reading the גמרא will test)
Its mark is visible (dry, but a stain can be seen)

phrases.english: If you say "soaked in" means it is no longer wet,
and "did not soak in" means it is still wet,
and Rabbi Yosei comes to say:
only as long as it is wet is it forbidden,
but if only its mark is visible, it is permitted,
that is the same as the first Tanna!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question in step 43 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the reading that נבלעו means 'no longer wet.'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under that reading the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי would hold the same view, leaving no dispute.

steps.title: 'Soaked in' means no mark is left, so they disagree about a visible mark
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads 'soaked in' as 'no visible mark,' so the תנא קמא forbids a visible mark and רבי יוסי permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, 'soaked in' means its mark is not visible, and 'did not soak in' means its mark is visible. And רבי יוסי comes to say that only while it is wet is it forbidden, but if only a mark is visible it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second meaning, which creates a real dispute. This seems to show that the question of a visible mark is an argument between תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the תנא קמא forbids urine as long as a mark can be seen, even if it is dry. רבי יוסי forbids it only while wet, so a dry visible mark is permitted. רבא's ruling in step 38 would then match רבי יוסי but not the תנא קמא.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this reading holds, רבא's ruling that only wet urine is forbidden would follow just one side of a dispute between תנאים.

phrases.english: Rather, "soaked in" means its mark is not visible,
and "did not soak in" means its mark is visible.
And Rabbi Yosei comes to say
only as long as it is wet is it forbidden,
but if only its mark is visible, it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second, accepted meaning after step 44 rejected the first.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: נבלעו means no visible mark; לא נבלעו means a visible mark. So the תנא קמא forbids a visible mark and רבי יוסי permits it.

steps.title: Maybe everyone agrees a visible mark is permitted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: perhaps both תנאים agree that only wet urine is forbidden and a visible mark is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees that only while it is wet is it forbidden, but if only a mark is visible it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to reject the idea that this is a dispute about a visible mark. It is setting up the next move, where it will explain what the תנאים really argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא claims both the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי permit a dry, visible mark. If that is true, the ברייתא is not a dispute about the mark at all, and רבא's ruling fits everyone. The explanation of what they do argue about comes on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not the end of the argument. The sentence ends with a comma, and the גמרא explains the real point of disagreement between the תנאים on the next amud.

phrases.english: No.
Everyone agrees
that only as long as it is wet is it forbidden,
but if only its mark is visible, it is permitted,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the conclusion of steps 42 and 45 that the תנאים argue about a visible mark.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא shows a dispute about a visible mark (לימא כתנאי).
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read so that both opinions permit a visible mark; their dispute must be about something else, still to be explained.
